chapter_theme: The first of the general songs (பொதுப்பாடல்கள், 1 of 21), named for no shrine: litanies of 'namo namah' to Murugan and to the goddess, the poet's long self-condemnations, pleas for the supreme truth beyond kingly pomp and beyond the quarrels of sects, Ganapati's offerings, the funeral drum, and yogic and doctrinal hymns.
structure_note: Litanies (992 to 994, 998, 1005), with 994 and 998 mostly naming the goddess; self-condemnations (993, 1003, 1006); songs against worldly pomp (995, 996, sharing a refrain) and against the sects (1004); pleas against women and death (997, 1001, 1002); and two songs that ask to sing and know the Lord (999, 1000).

992.reading: The poet hails Murugan in a litany of 'namo namah': knowledge beyond the gunas, lord of nada, the partless, the fullness of the kalas, cousin of Kama, kadamba-footed, son of the three Tamils and life of the three worlds, and asks whether, without falling at the lotus feet with that praise, he must drown in the ocean of seven births and whirl in Kama's maya. The praise piles up names: son of Siva who dances with vetalas in the forest, son of the Ganga, master of the elephant-raised maid, lord of the peacock, Visakha, six-faced, sporting with the hunter Lakshmi, slayer of Sura, and Vinayaka's dear brother.
992.nuance: The plea is short and sits inside the litany: the 'namo namah' is itself what the poet fears he will fail to say (என்று பாத வாரிஜத்தில் விழாதே). பஞ்சபாண பூபன் மைத்துன: Murugan as cousin of Kama, since Kama is Vishnu's son and Vishnu is Murugan's uncle.

993.reading: The poet condemns himself at length as one who never studied the three Tamils, useless, lustful, a demon of desire without the yoga of the indweller, fool of fools, a ruin who never sought the fruit of penance, a plotter of sin and killing, without justice, the greatest traitor among sinners, angry and greedy, a ruined jester living in the tangle of bonds, and asks when Murugan will take him. The praise is a litany of 'namo namah': the virtuous one with the golden trident, honey of the three Tamils, hard for Brahma to reach, dancer in the hall, the feet that trampled Death's messenger, the true guru of nada, light within the light, lord of the great gods.
993.nuance: The self-condemnation is formally a string of accusatives ending in -அனை (வ்ருதாவனை, காமாவிகாரனை, மோடாதி மோடனை), each a charge the poet lays on himself, closed by ஆளுவது எந்நாளோ. The second half answers it in the same rhythm with 'namo namah'.

994.reading: A litany without a plea: 'namo namah' to Murugan, knower of the Veda, hero of the vel, the lotus feet of bindu and nada, the peacock like a cloud, undivided knowledge, the one who became the elements and lives in fullness, twelve-armed. Then it names the goddess whom Lakshmi, Sarasvati, Indrani and the seven mothers serve, the vina-bearer, Siva's support, Adishakti, Parvati, Neeli, wearer of serpents, eternal mother, and hails Murugan as her son, slayer of Sura and life of the Veda-knowers.
994.nuance: பூதம் மற்றுமே ஆனாய், பூரணத்துளே வாழ்வாய்: Murugan as the elements and as the fullness within them. Nearly half the song is the goddess's names, and Murugan's praise is that he is the son of that Aryai.

995.reading: The poet asks whether he, who never grasped the supreme truth that guarding the soul is the highest state and the true aim of life, but wandered on elephants and horses with armies, houses, lands and forests, and spent night and day with women's dance, song and scented breasts, should lose this body so. The praise names Murugan who taught Siva, Parvati's lord, the initiation beyond waking, the poet of the four kinds of verse, son of the Krittikas, the six-lettered and twelve-eyed one, and the vel that felled Meru and made the demons roar and the sea cry out.
995.nuance: ஆவி காப்பதுமேற் பதமாதலாற் புருடார்த்தம் இதாம் எனாப் பரமார்த்தம்: the plea is philosophical, the soul's keeping as the true புருஷார்த்தம், against the pomp of rule and pleasure. சாக்ர அதீத தீக்ஷை: the initiation Murugan gives Siva is named as beyond the waking state. Several Sanskrit words in the praise are corrupt.

996.reading: The poet asks, before he loses his cruel body through craving for women and the weariness of boasting as a king, 'I am the tiger of the seven worlds', on horse, chariot and elephant, for the supreme truth he never understood in the guru's word that Siva is one and many, Siva-bliss and clarity. The praise names Murugan who became guru by one word of knowledge, hard for Vishnu on the serpent and for Brahma, who gives his state to poets who sing him with longing, and the vel that brought down the mountain of the demons while the sea cried out.
996.nuance: ஏகமாய்ப் பலவாய்ச் சிவபோகமாய்த் தெளிவாய்ச் சிவமீது எனா: the guru's word quoted is a compact Saiva creed, Siva as one and many. Like 995, which shares its refrain (வேலை கூப்பிட வீக்கிய பெருமாளே), it sets royal pride and desire against the truth not grasped. சோதி காட்ட அராச்சுத நாதனார்க்கு is unclear.

997.reading: The poet asks that his life not whirl in the fierce sorrow of fate, deluded by women whose kayal-fish eyes fight through their ear-rings and plunder life like spears, and asks for the manhood to worship the feet by Murugan's grace, so that this dog may live. The praise names the sun, moon, worlds and gods who bow, the vel that pierced Sura's chest, and Murugan who in a hunter's guise went to the millet field and said to the cloud-haired girl, 'hear me, you alone are my refuge'.
997.nuance: ஆண்மை தந்தருள்: the strength asked for is to worship, not to conquer. In the praise the god himself speaks Valli's refuge-formula to her (வேறு தஞ்சமும் நீயே), inverting the devotee's words.

998.reading: The poet describes the eight-petalled lotus of the world, with the sun on it, the deities set in their places, the yogic mantra of the mooladhara, the crowned seat above, the jewelled mansion known by the texts and countless lights, incense and lamps in a wide hall, and asks Murugan, the hero, pandit and acharya who ascended it, to remove his karma. Then a long list of the goddess's names, Kumari, Pingalai, Mangalai, Abhirami who danced in the hall, Kala-sankari, trident-bearer, dark-throated, skull-bearer, Kalyani, the text of the Vama tantra, Sivakamasundari, ends by hailing Murugan as her son.
998.nuance: The first half seems to describe the body's lotuses as a temple, with மூலாதாரம், the gods stationed in it and the crown above as the mandapa, but the syntax is a long list and the reading is tentative. The goddess's names include tantric ones (பிங்கலை, காம தந்திர, வாம தந்திர நூல்).

999.reading: The poet asks whether a day will come when he too, knowing it, praises Murugan, singing many verses: the one whom Brahma who spoke the Vedas and Vishnu of the bird could not find, the fire filling the sky, Siva of great fame, praised Murugan with love as great guru so that he might think on the feet. The praise lingers on Valli's eyes, lips, hair, breasts, waist and ear-leaf, and names Murugan who, saying 'this is the way', wandered alone and steadfast in her service, and the vel that struck the sea and Sura.
999.nuance: The first lines tell the column of fire that Brahma and Vishnu could not measure, and then make that Siva praise Murugan as guru. The plea is for the gift of song and knowing, as in 2 and 25. The praise's word சாதனம் is unclear.

1000.reading: The poet tells how Valli, guarding the millet on her platform, was stirred by love, and Murugan entered the field, and asks whether a day will come when, singing that valour and calling to the poets so that all the land knows, he gains the rare penance to seek the two feet praised by the fourteen worlds. The praise names Vishnu who churned the sea with Mandara and the serpent for rope and fed the hungry gods, Siva who burned the forts and bent the great mountain as bow, the gods' cry 'you bore our burden', the demons destroyed, Indra freed from prison, and Murugan who resettled heaven.
1000.nuance: அருந்தவம் வாய்ப்பதும் ஒருநாளே: the penance hoped for is to sing Murugan's valour in the Valli story, praise itself as the tapas. The division of the first half's syntax is uncertain.

1001.reading: The poet confesses the infatuation for women's eyes, voice, hair, waist, gait, lips, smile and musk-scented breasts that never abates, and pictures the end: disease, Yama taking the life, mourners fondling, weeping and fainting, someone calling 'take away the old corpse', a drum beating, and the walk to the burning ground, and asks whether that is sweet. The praise names Rama, who cut off ten heads and twenty arms with one arrow, Vishnu who answered the elephant in the pond and drank out the demoness's life with her milk, and who measured the worlds with his feet, and the vel that shattered the northern peak.
1001.nuance: The question இனிதோ தான், 'is that sweet?', turns the lover's word back on him at the funeral. குதறு முதுபிணம் எடும் என: the mourners themselves call the body an old corpse to be taken away.

1002.reading: The poet lists the offerings to Ganapati, chickpeas, lentils, flattened and puffed rice, sweets, vadai, plantain and many fruits, set before the great-bellied elephant god with gladness, and confesses that he has not bowed with folded hands and streaming eyes to the one who comes after him, Muruga, Shanmukha; he asks whether his wandering in cruel karma, poverty, smallness and the pit of women will not end. The praise shows Death and sun and moon afraid as the vel, the peacock that circles the world and the cry 'Hara Hara' of sages and gods, and ends with Murugan grown in the Saravana pool.
1002.nuance: The worship of Ganapati is laid out in full and Murugan is named as the one who comes after (பிறகு வரும் ஒரு முருக), the order of temple worship; the fault confessed is to have stopped short of bowing to him. Poverty (வறுமை) is named among the sufferings, unusual beside the women.

1003.reading: The poet describes the courtesans, proud, foolish, deceitful thieves who draw young men into the net of their quarrelsome eyes and melt them like wax in fire, and confesses that, seeking them, he never even tried to follow the words of the great virtuous ones who teach the ascetic state, so that his kin and all people call him a fool and low-born; he asks, since this servant suffers so, to be given the one rare meaning. The praise shows Siva dancing to the damaru while sages melt crying 'Hara', names Murugan as son of the goddess who dwells with him, Kumara, Saravanabhava, guru on the peacock, who embraced Valli.
1003.nuance: The poet reports what others say of him (அசடன் அறிவிலி இழிகுலன் இவன் என இனமும் மனிதருள் அனைவரும் உரைசெய), a public shame rather than a private confession. The cure asked for is a teaching (ஒரு பொருள்), in keeping with the neglect of the sages' words.

1004.reading: The poet asks Murugan to leave behind the path of those who tend the little hut of a body of flesh, blood and worms bound for the cremation ground: the ritualists, the quarrelling sectarians, and those of half-grown knowledge who call chariyai and kiriyai penance, and to tell him plainly 'this is the thing', so that the two deeds, the malas, night and day, 'mine' and 'yours' all cease, and the experience of that sweet solitude, beyond what the Vedas' end can fix, the greatness of two in one, is revealed. The praise names the goddess, daughter of the mountain king, worshipped by the seven mothers, Abhirami of Arunai who gave the seven nether worlds, and Murugan her son, who gave Pasupati the one word of silence, with his consorts, vel, peacock, poetry, the sweet verse of the Upanishads, generosity and beauty.
1004.nuance: இரவு பகலற எனதற நினதற அநுபூதி: the state asked for is named by what ceases, and the word அநுபூதி (direct experience) is the goal. Chariyai and kiriyai are here among the paths to be left, though in 979 the poet longs for them. மவுனம் அருளிய: the teaching to Siva is given as silence, not as Om.

1005.reading: The poet asks whether a day will come when he can speak without fault all the names that come as 'Muruga, the six-faced', telling the peacock that crushed the northern peak, the seven hills and the serpent king's hoods, the rooster banner, Murugan's compassion, greatness, colour, youth, the two feet, the kadamba crown and the shoulders that embraced Valli. The praise sounds the vel against the demons, the blood river, the sea torn and the mango tree felled, and the hill named for a bird pierced, and names Murugan guru, Saravana, whom the Ganga, the six women and Uma each call 'my child'.
1005.nuance: The plea is the wish to praise rightly (பழுதற மொழிவது), and the list of what is to be praised is the song. குருகு பெயரிய வரை is the Krauncha hill, named for the heron; the mango (அடுமரம்) is Sura.

1006.reading: The poet condemns himself at length: without a millet-grain's thought of sharing, without compassion, who never sang Arunai, Thanigai, Palani, Swamimalai and the many hills, deceitful of speech, without beauty, caste, goodness or the medicine for birth, a mind that whirls seventy times in one turn of the potter's wheel, who never thought to melt, weep and worship, darkened, graceless, without wealth, a thief, without mind, path or rule, and asks whether a day will come for him to reach Siva's state. The praise names Vishnu at length, Rama who cut Ravana's heads and arms with one arrow, the royal envoy, the giver to the elephant in the pond, the one who fought the twin marutha trees, the man-lion who tore Hiranya when his child prattled the Veda, the dancer on the serpent's hood, and Murugan the sun of devotees who circled the world in an instant.
1006.nuance: The list is built of words in -இலி (one without): கருணையிலி, அழகிலி, குலமிலி, அருளிலி, விதியிலி, and the first lack named is sharing (பகிர நினைவு ஒரு தினையளவிலும் இலி). திகிரி வரும் ஒரு செலவினில் எழுபது செலவு வரு மன பவுரி: the mind spins seventy times while the potter's wheel turns once.

links.note: Twin songs with one refrain: both set the pomp of riding elephants and horses as a king, and pleasure with women, against the supreme truth (பரமார்த்தம்) never grasped, and both name Murugan as Siva's teacher.

In 979 the poet longs to leave praise-poetry for a life of chariyai and kiriyai; in 1004 those who call chariyai and kiriyai penance are among the half-knowers whose path he asks to leave for the experience beyond deeds and malas. The two fit as stages, not as a contradiction.

Both set the quarrels of the sects against knowing the light within: Tirumular says that for one who reaches it there is no quarrel at all, and 1004 asks to leave the quarrelling sectarians for an experience where 'mine' and 'yours' cease.

Both stand the lover of pleasure beside the funeral: the Naladiyar's drum answers the man who sees the corpse carried yet thinks there is joy here, and 1001 asks at the drum and the burning ground whether that is sweet.

Both measure the failure to give by a millet grain: 23 asks to share even a grain of millet before Death's summons, and 1006 opens its self-condemnation with having not a millet-grain's thought of sharing.
